title: Four chat tools, four different jobs

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: If someone says they need live chat for their website, which product should they buy? Antoine's answer is that it depends on the job, not the logo.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Fair, but they all do chat, don't they?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Not really. He wrote these notes while helping a bilingual storefront team pick live chat, a bot, and something agents could actually work from. The four products he looked at aren't interchangeable.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: 3CX is a phone system at heart, with web chat in the same queue. If you already run voice on it, that's one vendor and one agent desk. The catch is you're buying a communications platform, not a neutral helpdesk.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Conversational marketing, leaning hard on Instagram and Facebook. Great for growth flows and lead capture. Not what you want for a support desk with email, phone and web in one place.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Kommunicate is bot first, human when it matters. The bot takes the first turn, then hands off to an agent, and it's managed SaaS, so no server to run. Chatwoot is an open-source shared inbox. You can use their cloud or self-host with Docker.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: It can cut per-seat cost, but then you own backups, upgrades and security. And voice may lag behind the big proprietary suites.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So which one won for that team?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: No vendor won every row. He scored on agent training time, French and English inbox, who owns the server, and whether marketing owns the bot. The winner was the least new moving parts, which is why 3CX and Chatwoot came up most.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: They do, and the page says so. Use it as a map, then confirm with each vendor. The full write-up has the decision flowchart and a comparison table.
